submission.natural_language_explanation: L1/N660+ is a word-assembly (detokenisation) detector: it fires where a word or technical identifier is split across several BPE pieces, peaking on short, 1-3 character, non-initial pieces that carry the word's orthographic core - Greek accented 'i' inside opo[[i]]o, the elision apostrophe in qu[[']]en, 'ir' in adm[[ir]]ably, 'st' in fanta[[st]]ico, 'ch' in per[[ch]]e, 'er' in hab[[er]], 'ar' in overdecl[[ar]]atie, 'ed' in st[[ed]], and identifier pieces 'css' and ' ADVIS' - with the preceding stem piece contributing as much as the peak token itself. Whole word-initial tokens and words that fit in a single token are weak or silent (the two word-initial peaks, 'What the devil' and 'you meet', are unmodelled leftovers), and its value direction promotes long multi-morphemic academic words (' hierarch', ' asymmetry', ' kinematics', ' evolutionary') while suppressing long whitespace/indentation runs.

rival_explanations: The pole is simply a token-identity detector for about a dozen frequent BPE fragments, so it should be near zero on any fragment outside that list even in the same mid-word position (for example 'ablish' inside re|establish or 'ic' inside publ|ic), which the word-assembly reading predicts should fire.

The pole is a non-English multi-byte/diacritic detector, so it should fire just as strongly on word-initial accented tokens such as ' Έ' or on short accented words like 'déjà', which the word-assembly reading predicts are weak.

The pole tracks rare high-content vocabulary density rather than word-internal position, so it should fire on word-initial rare academic words with a leading space (e.g. ' Heidegger', ' kinematics', ' asymmetry') and stay quiet on common-word fragments such as 'er' in haber or 'ed' in steed.

ESA invites European schools to join together to observe the transit of Mercury taking place on Monday 9 May 2016. Schools are challenged to observe the transit and to recreate the measurements made by astronomers around 300 years ago in order to calculate the distance between the Earth and the Sun.
Updates have been made to this page and can be found below.
A transit occurs when a one celestial object passes in front of another. From our viewpoint on Earth, it can only be the two innermost planets in the Solar System, Mercury and Venus that transit the disc of the Sun.
A transit of Mercury is a relatively rare event happening only 13 or 14 times each century. Mercury actually passes between the Earth and Sun at least three times a year, however since its orbit is inclined with respect to the plane of the Solar System, it usually appears to pass above or below the Sun to an observer on Earth.
During a transit, Mercury appears as a small black dot moving across the disc of the Sun.
On 9 May 2016, from 11:12 until 18:42 UT, an entire transit of Mercury will be visible from western Europe. Find out if you can enjoy this event from your location, here.
ESA invites European schools to observe the transit of Mercury (either the entire or partial transit) and to measure the times that the edge of the disc of Mercury makes contact with the edge of the disc of the Sun.
To be able to calculate the distance between the Earth and the Sun from the transit you will need a second set of data from a different location, ideally as far away as possible. Therefore, we would like you to send your data to us so that it can be made available to everyone participating.
Send your data to share here.
Data from all participants and other transit of Mercury observers will be available here.
There are many different ways to calculate the distance between the Earth and the Sun using a transit. Find out more here.
Once you have calculated the distance between the Earth and the Sun Earth-Sun from your measurements, you can submit a short report of your transit of Mercury experience to be published on the ESA website, and be in with a chance of winning a prize. Your report should include a brief description of your observing event with a picture, and your calculations as well as your result.
Deadline for submission of reports extended to Monday 6 June 2016.
Submit a report of your transit of Mercury experience here.
Even if you are not able to make your own observations you can still submit a report and calculate the distance between the Earth and the Sun using the measurements that will be published online.
If you are observing the event please remember to NEVER look at the Sun with unprotected eyes, through ordinary sunglasses or through a telescope, as this might cause permanent damage to your eyes.

adversarial_test_results.detail: New Spanish sentence whose split points are pieces such as 'res'|'olver' and 'gob'|'ierno', with no diacritic or multi-byte token anywhere; the word-assembly reading predicts firing, the diacritic rival predicts silence, and the token-identity rival sees none of its dozen fragments.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Quiero comer algo antes de salir, y luego podemos beber algo en el bar de la esquina.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Ordinary Spanish sentence whose split points are the exact 'er' piece in comer and the exact 'ir' piece in salir; word-assembly and token-identity both predict firing, the rare-vocabulary rival predicts silence on such plain words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The results were unbelievably clear, so the committee ended the debate before the vote.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The insurance policy will indemnify the owner if the building is hit by fire or flood during the winter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The short non-initial piece 'ify' inside indemn|ify is outside the claimed dozen, so the word-assembly reading predicts firing while the token-identity rival predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Greek prose on a new topic in which the accented 'ί' recurs as a non-initial piece (φωτογραφίες); word-assembly and the Greek/diacritic rival predict firing, the rare-vocabulary rival predicts silence on plain vocabulary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: L'homme qui habitait à côté est parti sans laisser d'adresse, et personne ne sait où il est.
adversarial_test_results.detail: French elision apostrophes in new words (L'', d'') rather than the example's qu'en; the hypothesis predicts firing on the bare elision apostrophe, and the diacritic rival also fires on à and où.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: An ADVISORY note was pinned to the door this morning, warning that the office would close early.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Uppercase identifier piece ' ADVIS' inside ADVISORY in a procedural register unlike the examples; the hypothesis predicts firing on that piece.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Common-vocabulary Spanish sentence whose split points are pieces like 'v'|'ender' and 'trab'|'ajo' rather than any claimed fragment; word-assembly predicts firing, the token-identity rival sees none of its dozen fragments, and the rare-vocabulary rival predicts silence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The Lessee shall indemnify the Lessor against any claims arising from the use of the premises during the term of this agreement.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Legal-register sentence, a genre absent from the scan corpus, with mid-word pieces ('see', 'ify', 'or') outside the claimed list; word-assembly predicts firing, token-identity predicts silence, and the rare-vocabulary rival fires on the legal lexis.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He said that he would go to the store and buy some milk and bread for the family before it got dark, and then he would come back home.

readings.explanation: L1/N660+ is a word-assembly (detokenisation) detector: it fires where a word or technical identifier is split across several BPE pieces, peaking on short, 1-3 character, non-initial pieces that carry the word's orthographic core - Greek accented 'i' inside opo[[i]]o, the elision apostrophe in qu[[']]en, 'ir' in adm[[ir]]ably, 'st' in fanta[[st]]ico, 'ch' in per[[ch]]e, 'er' in hab[[er]], 'ar' in overdecl[[ar]]atie, 'ed' in st[[ed]], and identifier pieces 'css' and ' ADVIS' - with the preceding stem piece contributing as much as the peak token itself. Whole word-initial tokens and words that fit in a single token are weak or silent (the two word-initial peaks, 'What the devil' and 'you meet', are unmodelled leftovers), and its value direction promotes long multi-morphemic academic words (' hierarch', ' asymmetry', ' kinematics', ' evolutionary') while suppressing long whitespace/indentation runs.

The pole is simply a token-identity detector for about a dozen frequent BPE fragments, so it should be near zero on any fragment outside that list even in the same mid-word position (for example 'ablish' inside re|establish or 'ic' inside publ|ic), which the word-assembly reading predicts should fire.

The pole is a non-English multi-byte/diacritic detector, so it should fire just as strongly on word-initial accented tokens such as ' Έ' or on short accented words like 'déjà', which the word-assembly reading predicts are weak.

The pole tracks rare high-content vocabulary density rather than word-internal position, so it should fire on word-initial rare academic words with a leading space (e.g. ' Heidegger', ' kinematics', ' asymmetry') and stay quiet on common-word fragments such as 'er' in haber or 'ed' in steed.
